title: The Antibiotic Revolution
summary: Follow the discovery of sulfa drugs, penicillin and streptomycin, and the early warnings of bacterial resistance.

lessons.title: Domagk and Prontosil: The First Sulfa Drug (1935)

levels.kid:
Long ago, a tiny scratch or a sore throat could turn into a germ infection that made people very sick. Doctors had no medicine that could stop germs hiding inside the body.

A German scientist named **Gerhard Domagk** wanted to fix that. He worked at a company that made bright dyes for cloth. Chemists there made a red dye called **Prontosil**. Domagk gave it to mice that had a germ infection. The mice that got the red dye lived!

Later his own daughter got a bad infection in her arm, and the red medicine helped her get better.

Then scientists found something surprising. The body breaks the red dye apart. One small piece, called **sulfanilamide**, does the real germ-fighting. It looks like germ food, so it tricks the germs, and they stop growing.
levels.hs:
Before the mid-1930s, doctors had almost no drugs that could cure a bacterial infection inside the body. A strep throat, an infected wound, or **puerperal fever** (also called childbed fever, an infection of the uterus after giving birth) could kill a healthy young person.

**Gerhard Domagk**, a German physician-scientist, led the bacteriology lab at **Bayer**, part of the chemical giant IG Farben. Bayer chemists Josef Klarer and Fritz Mietzsch made hundreds of **azo dyes**. Domagk tested them in mice infected with deadly **streptococci**. In 1932 one red dye carrying a **sulfonamide** group, later named **Prontosil**, protected the mice, while untreated mice died. Domagk published the results in 1935.

The strange part: Prontosil did nothing to bacteria in a test tube. Later in 1935, a team at the **Pasteur Institute** in Paris showed why. The body splits Prontosil and releases a colorless molecule, **sulfanilamide**, which is the real antibacterial. A drug that has to be converted in the body before it works is called a **prodrug**.

Sulfanilamide works by imitating **PABA**, a building block bacteria use to make the vitamin **folate**. Starved of folate, bacteria stop multiplying, and the immune system clears them.

In 1936 Leonard Colebrook in London reported far fewer deaths from childbed fever in women treated with the new drug. Domagk was awarded the 1939 Nobel Prize, but the Nazi government forced him to decline it.
levels.college:
**The problem.** In the early 1930s, chemotherapy meant a few special cases: Ehrlich's arsenical Salvarsan for syphilis and quinine for malaria. Nothing reliably cured common bacterial killers such as streptococcal sepsis, pneumonia or meningitis.

**The screen.** At Bayer's Elberfeld laboratories, Domagk ran an **in vivo screen**. Mice were infected with a virulent *Streptococcus pyogenes* strain and given compounds made by chemists Josef Klarer and Fritz Mietzsch. Azo dyes were chosen because dyes bind selectively to tissues and microbes, the idea behind Ehrlich's 'magic bullet.' Adding a sulfonamide group (-SO2NH2) produced compound KL 730, patented in 1932 and sold as **Prontosil**. Domagk announced it in 1935 in *Deutsche Medizinische Wochenschrift*.

**The prodrug twist.** Prontosil is inactive in vitro. In late 1935, Jacques and Therese Trefouel, Federico Nitti and Daniel Bovet, working in Ernest Fourneau's lab at the Pasteur Institute, showed that the body cleaves the azo bond and releases **sulfanilamide**. Sulfanilamide had been synthesized by Paul Gelmo in 1908 and was not protected by any useful patent, so any company could make it. A worldwide 'sulfa craze' followed.

**Mechanism.**
- Sulfanilamide is a structural analog of **para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)**.
- It competitively inhibits **dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS)**, an early enzyme in bacterial folate synthesis.
- Without folate, bacteria cannot make thymidine and purines for DNA, so they stop dividing. The effect is **bacteriostatic**: host defenses finish the job.
- **Selective toxicity**: human cells lack DHPS and absorb ready-made folate from food.

**Impact.** Sulfonamides cut deaths from puerperal fever, pneumococcal pneumonia (sulfapyridine, 'M&B 693', 1938) and meningococcal meningitis. In 1936, Franklin D. Roosevelt Jr. recovered from a severe streptococcal throat infection after sulfa treatment, making headlines across the United States. Domagk was named the 1939 Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine, but a Nazi decree forced him to refuse; he received the medal in 1947.
levels.phd:
**Biochemistry.** DHPS (encoded by *folP*) condenses PABA with 6-hydroxymethyl-7,8-dihydropterin pyrophosphate to form 7,8-dihydropteroate. Dihydrofolate synthase then adds glutamate, and dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) yields tetrahydrofolate, the one-carbon carrier needed for thymidylate, purines and methionine. Sulfonamides compete with PABA at the active site, and some are themselves condensed with the pterin to form dead-end sulfa-pterin adducts. Because cells hold existing folate stores, growth inhibition appears only after a lag of several generations.

**The antimetabolite theory.** In 1940 Donald Woods, working with Paul Fildes, showed that PABA (present in yeast extract) reverses sulfanilamide's effect in a competitive fashion. Fildes generalized this into the **antimetabolite** concept: a drug can act by mimicking an essential metabolite. This idea later guided Hitchings and Elion's rational design of purine and folate antagonists. The same logic explained a clinical puzzle: sulfonamides work poorly in pus and necrotic tissue, where breakdown of host cells and bacteria supplies PABA and thymidine that bypass the block.

**Why in vivo screening mattered.** Prontosil's azo bond is reductively cleaved by azoreductases in the liver and by gut bacteria. A test-tube screen would have discarded it. Domagk's insistence on infected animals, rather than culture plates, was decisive.

**Historiography and controversy.** Historians such as John Lesch (*The First Miracle Drugs*, 2007) and Thomas Hager (*The Demon Under the Microscope*, 2006) note the gap between the 1932 mouse results and 1935 publication. One interpretation is that Bayer delayed while securing patents on a proprietary dye. The Pasteur group's finding that the cheap, unpatentable sulfanilamide was the active agent undercut that commercial strategy. Whether Bayer's chemists already suspected the cleavage remains debated.

**Early resistance.** Sulfonamide-resistant gonococci and streptococci were reported during the Second World War, within a decade of introduction. Mechanisms include *folP* mutations lowering sulfonamide affinity while preserving PABA binding, PABA overproduction, and acquired genes (*sul1*, *sul2*, *sul3*) encoding drug-insensitive DHPS. *sul1* sits in class 1 integrons and is now among the most widespread resistance genes in environmental and clinical bacteria.
levels.expert:
**Sequential blockade.** Sulfonamides survive clinically mainly in combination. Trimethoprim, a bacterial DHFR inhibitor from the Hitchings program, paired with sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) inhibits two consecutive steps of folate synthesis, giving synergy and often bactericidal activity. Current uses include *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis, urinary tract infections, community MRSA skin infections and *Stenotrophomonas*. For the neuro-minded: cerebral toxoplasmosis is classically treated with pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine, another sequential blockade, and sulfonamides penetrate cerebrospinal fluid well, which is why they mattered so much for meningococcal meningitis.

**Adverse effects clinicians watch for:**
- Severe cutaneous reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
- Crystalluria and kidney injury, a problem from the early sulfa era.
- Hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
- Kernicterus risk in newborns, because sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin.
- With trimethoprim, hyperkalemia via blockade of epithelial sodium channels in the distal nephron.

**The 'sulfa allergy' pitfall.** Antibiotic sulfonamides carry an N4 arylamine and an N1 heterocyclic ring linked to hypersensitivity; most non-antibiotic sulfonamides lack both. Strom and colleagues (NEJM, 2003) found that patients who reacted to sulfonamide antibiotics did react more often to non-antibiotic sulfonamides, but reacted even more often to penicillins. This points to a general allergy-prone tendency rather than true structural cross-reactivity, and reflexively withholding useful drugs from patients labeled sulfa-allergic is usually unjustified.

**Chemical descendants.** Sulfanilamide's side effect of metabolic acidosis was traced to carbonic anhydrase inhibition (Mann and Keilin, 1940). That line led to acetazolamide, which reduces CSF production and is used in idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and then to thiazide and loop diuretics. Marcel Janbon's 1942 observation of hypoglycemia in typhoid patients given a sulfonamide in Montpellier seeded the sulfonylureas for diabetes.

**Regulatory shadow.** The 1937 Elixir Sulfanilamide tragedy, a liquid formulation made with toxic diethylene glycol, drove the 1938 US Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (covered in a later unit).

**Open questions.** Plasmid-borne *sul* genes persist widely in soil, water and gut microbiota despite falling sulfonamide use, which challenges the hope that resistance fades once a drug is withdrawn. Structure-guided work targeting the conserved pterin pocket of DHPS seeks inhibitors that escape existing resistance.

lessons.title: Fleming's Mold: The Discovery of Penicillin (1928)

levels.kid:
In 1928, a scientist named **Alexander Fleming** came back from a summer holiday to his messy lab in London. Before he left, he had set out dishes of germs called **bacteria**.

On one dish, a fuzzy blue-green **mold** had grown. It was the same kind of fuzz you might see on old bread. Something strange had happened, though. All around the mold, the germs were gone! It was as if the mold had built an invisible fence.

Fleming guessed that the mold was making a special juice that hurt germs. He named it **penicillin**. It did not seem to hurt the body's own cells.

But he could not make enough of it to use as medicine. Other scientists solved that problem later. Then penicillin saved millions of lives.
levels.hs:
In September 1928, **Alexander Fleming**, a bacteriologist at St Mary's Hospital in London, returned from holiday and sorted through old culture plates of **Staphylococcus**, a bacterium that causes boils and wound infections. One plate had been contaminated by a mold. Around the mold, the staph colonies had turned see-through and were dissolving. Colonies farther away looked normal.

Fleming grew the mold in broth. He showed that the liquid, which he first called 'mould juice,' killed or stopped many bacteria. In 1929 he named the active substance **penicillin**, after the mold's genus, **Penicillium**. His 1929 paper reported that:
- It worked against many **Gram-positive** bacteria, such as staph and streptococci, and also against gonococci and meningococci.
- It had little effect on others, such as *E. coli* and *Haemophilus influenzae*.
- It did not harm white blood cells. Harsh **antiseptics** like carbolic acid (phenol) did harm them.

Penicillin is an **antibiotic**: a substance made by one microbe that kills or stops other microbes.

Fleming did not turn it into a medicine. It was unstable and hard to purify, so he mainly used it as a lab tool for sorting out bacteria. About a decade later, a team at Oxford finished the job.

Luck mattered, but so did noticing the plate. As Louis Pasteur said, 'chance favours only the prepared mind.'
levels.college:
**The prepared mind.** Fleming worked in Sir Almroth Wright's Inoculation Department at St Mary's, a lab focused on vaccines and immunity. During World War I he had shown that chemical antiseptics poured into deep wounds killed the patient's **leukocytes** (white blood cells) faster than they killed bacteria. In 1921 he discovered **lysozyme**, a natural antibacterial enzyme in nasal mucus and tears. Lysozyme mostly destroyed harmless bacteria, but it trained him to look for natural substances that dissolve bacteria.

**The observation (1928).** On a staphylococcal plate contaminated by a *Penicillium* mold, colonies near the mold had undergone **lysis**, meaning they had burst and become transparent.

**Fleming's experiments (1928-29):**
- Filtered broth inhibited staphylococci even when diluted roughly 1 in 800.
- Sensitive: streptococci, staphylococci, pneumococci, the diphtheria bacillus, gonococci and meningococci. Insensitive: coliforms such as *E. coli*, typhoid bacilli and *H. influenzae*.
- It was non-toxic when injected into mice and rabbits and did not damage leukocytes in vitro.
- Discouraging findings: killing took hours, injected penicillin largely disappeared from rabbit blood within about 30 minutes, and the active agent lost potency quickly. His assistants Stuart Craddock and Frederick Ridley managed only partial concentration.

**Mechanism (worked out decades later).** Penicillin is a **beta-lactam**. It inactivates **penicillin-binding proteins** (transpeptidases) that cross-link **peptidoglycan**, the mesh of the bacterial cell wall. Bacteria that are actively growing keep building weakened wall and then burst, which explains the lysis Fleming saw. Human cells have no peptidoglycan. In Gram-negatives, the **outer membrane** limits access, which helps explain the resistance of coliforms.

**Why it stalled.** Fleming's 1929 paper in the *British Journal of Experimental Pathology* stressed using penicillin in culture media to isolate *H. influenzae*, which survived while competing bacteria died. In 1930, Cecil Paine in Sheffield used crude filtrate to cure several eye infections in newborns. In 1932, Harold Raistrick's chemists tried to extract it and found it too unstable. Systemic therapy waited for Florey and Chain at Oxford.
levels.phd:
**Reconstructing the accident.** The famous plate is less straightforward than it looks. Penicillin lyses only growing bacteria, so a mold spore landing on a mature staphylococcal lawn should do nothing. In the 1970s Ronald Hare, a former colleague of Fleming, reconstructed a plausible sequence. The plate was seeded before Fleming's holiday and left on the bench at room temperature. A cool spell in London that summer favored the mold's growth over the staphylococci's. The mold became established and secreted penicillin, and warmer weather then let the staphylococci grow, except within the diffusion zone. The likely spore source was C. J. La Touche's mycology lab on the floor below. The popular story that the spore came through an open window is probably false.

**The organism.** La Touche first identified the mold as *P. rubrum*, and Charles Thom later classified it as *P. notatum*. Genome-based taxonomy (Houbraken, Frisvad and Samson, 2011) placed Fleming's strain in *Penicillium rubens*. It was a low producer, which is part of why yields were hopeless.

**Precedents.** Microbial antagonism was not new:
- John Tyndall (1875) noted *Penicillium* clearing bacterial broths.
- Paul Vuillemin coined 'antibiosis' (1889).
- Ernest Duchesne's 1897 thesis described *Penicillium* protecting guinea pigs.
- André Gratia and Sara Dath (1925) saw a mold lyse staphylococci.

Fleming's distinction was naming, characterizing and distributing the agent.

**Biosynthesis.** The **ACV synthetase** (gene *pcbAB*), a nonribosomal peptide synthetase, condenses L-α-aminoadipate, L-cysteine and L-valine, epimerizing valine to its D form. **Isopenicillin N synthase** (*pcbC*), an iron-dependent oxidase, closes both the beta-lactam and thiazolidine rings in one step. An acyltransferase (*penDE*) swaps the side chain to give, for example, benzylpenicillin.

**Target.** Tipper and Strominger (1965) proposed that penicillin mimics the acyl-D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the peptidoglycan stem peptide. The strained beta-lactam acylates the active-site serine of transpeptidases, forming a long-lived covalent adduct.

**Nuance.** The rapid loss from blood Fleming saw in rabbits reflects fast renal tubular secretion. His 1929 paper did suggest penicillin might be useful when applied to, or injected into, infected areas, so he did not abandon therapy entirely. The wartime press nonetheless cast him as the sole hero, a credit dispute later softened by the shared 1945 Nobel Prize.
levels.expert:
Fleming's discovery left methods and concepts that are still in daily use.

**Methods that persist:**
- **Ditch plate to disc diffusion.** Fleming cut a gutter in agar, filled it with mold broth, and streaked test organisms across it to map sensitivity. Zone-of-inhibition testing, standardized later as Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion, still guides antibiotic choice. One pitfall: zone size depends on diffusion, inoculum density and growth rate, not only on intrinsic potency.
- **Selective media.** His use of penicillin to isolate *H. influenzae* has descendants in penicillin-streptomycin cell-culture media and in ampicillin selection of plasmid-bearing *E. coli* through the *bla* resistance gene.

**Pharmacology lessons:**
- **Selective toxicity.** Because the target is absent in humans, the therapeutic window is wide. The dominant clinical problem became hypersensitivity. Today about 10% of patients carry a penicillin-allergy label, yet over 90% of those tested tolerate penicillin. Unverified labels push clinicians toward broader agents, so allergy delabeling is a major stewardship priority.
- **Clearance.** The rapid elimination Fleming saw led to wartime use of probenecid to block tubular secretion and stretch scarce supplies.

**Neuro relevance.** Penicillin crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly unless the meninges are inflamed. Neurosurgeons noticed early that it is **epileptogenic** when it reaches cortex directly. A. Earl Walker reported convulsions after cortical application in the mid-1940s. The mechanism is **GABA-A receptor antagonism**, and topical cortical penicillin became a classic experimental model of focal seizures. The same property makes direct intrathecal or intraventricular use hazardous.

**Discovery science.** Fleming observed rather than screened. Systematic soil screening came later. Most environmental microbes still resist lab culture. Growing soil bacteria in situ with the iChip yielded teixobactin (Ling et al., 2015), and genome mining is now waking 'silent' biosynthetic gene clusters.

**Open questions:**
- Why do fungi make beta-lactams at all? Possibilities include competition and, as Julian Davies argued, signaling at sub-inhibitory concentrations.
- Can serendipity be engineered through high-throughput phenotypic assays?

**Historiography pitfall.** The tidy 'lucky accident' narrative hides how much depended on temperature, timing and a decade of other people's chemistry.

lessons.title: Florey, Chain and Heatley Turn Penicillin into a Medicine

levels.kid:
Fleming found a mold that could kill germs. But he had only a tiny bit of its juice, and the germ-killer in it fell apart easily. Ten years later, a team in Oxford, England, decided to try again.

- **Howard Florey** was the leader.
- **Ernst Chain** was a chemist who loved puzzles.
- **Norman Heatley** was a clever inventor who could build almost anything.

They grew mold in bedpans, bathtubs and special pots. Heatley built a machine from glass tubes and bottles to pull the medicine out of the mold juice.

Then they tested it on eight sick mice. The mice without medicine died. The mice with medicine lived!

Their first human patient got better at first. Then they ran out of medicine, and he got sick again. So they asked American factories to help make much more.
levels.hs:
Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, but he could not purify it, and few people expected it to become a medicine. About ten years later, a team at the **Sir William Dunn School of Pathology** at the University of Oxford took up the challenge.

The key people:
- **Howard Florey**, an Australian pathologist who led the team and raised money, partly from the Rockefeller Foundation.
- **Ernst Chain**, a German-born Jewish biochemist who had fled the Nazis. He found Fleming's 1929 paper and pushed to study penicillin.
- **Norman Heatley**, a biochemist and brilliant improviser who solved the practical problems.

Penicillin was fragile: it broke down quickly, especially in acid. Heatley found a way to **extract** it, moving it from the mold broth into a solvent and back into water, while keeping everything cold. He also invented a way to measure how strong each batch was. The team grew mold in bedpans, milk churns and custom ceramic vessels.

On 25 May 1940, they infected eight mice with deadly streptococcus bacteria and treated four with penicillin. The untreated mice died overnight; the treated mice survived. The results appeared in The Lancet that August.

In February 1941, an Oxford policeman, **Albert Alexander**, dying of a severe infection, became the first patient treated. He improved dramatically, but the supply ran out and he died. The team realized they needed factory-scale production, which came from the United States.
levels.college:
Turning a laboratory curiosity into a drug required solving three problems: purification, proof of efficacy, and supply.

**Why Oxford took it up.** In 1938 Florey and Chain planned a systematic study of natural antibacterial substances. Chain, reading Fleming's 1929 report, saw penicillin's instability as a biochemical puzzle worth solving. With Rockefeller Foundation support, work continued as Britain entered the Second World War.

**Purification.** Penicillin is an organic acid. Heatley's **back-extraction** exploited this: acidify the cold broth so penicillin becomes uncharged and moves into an organic solvent (ether, later amyl acetate), then shake it back into a neutral water buffer, leaving many impurities behind. Because penicillin decomposes at low pH, each step had to be fast and cold; Heatley built a countercurrent apparatus from glass tubing, bottles and spare parts. He also devised the **cylinder-plate assay**, measuring zones of inhibited bacterial growth to define a standard Oxford unit.

**Proof in animals.** In the May 1940 mouse protection test, the untreated mice infected with streptococci died within hours, while the treated mice survived the night. The 1940 Lancet paper also showed the extract was remarkably nontoxic to animals and to white blood cells, unlike chemical antiseptics.

**First patients.** Early human injections caused fevers from impurities (**pyrogens**), which further purification removed. Constable Albert Alexander's temporary recovery in 1941 proved clinical activity; a 1941 Lancet series, including children, confirmed it.

**Scale-up.** Wartime Britain lacked industrial capacity. In 1941 Florey and Heatley flew to the US. At the USDA Northern Regional Research Laboratory in **Peoria, Illinois**, Andrew Moyer found that **corn steep liquor** and lactose boosted yields, and submerged deep-tank fermentation replaced shallow surface cultures. Companies including Merck, Squibb and Pfizer scaled production in time for the 1944 Normandy invasion.

In 1945 Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
levels.phd:
The Oxford programme shows how chemistry, assay design and microbiology had to mature together.

**Chemical instability.** Penicillin's lability had defeated earlier workers, including Harold Raistrick's group in 1932, who extracted it into ether but lost activity. The reason became clear later: the strained four-membered **β-lactam** ring, fused to a thiazolidine ring, is highly reactive and hydrolyses in acid and alkali. That same reactivity underlies its mechanism.

**Assay first.** Without a quantitative assay, fractions cannot be compared. Heatley's cylinder-plate method, in which solution diffuses from small cylinders on a seeded agar plate and inhibition-zone diameter tracks concentration, let purification be followed step by step. Early broth held only a few units per millilitre, and the material used in 1940-41 was very impure by later standards, yet strikingly potent.

**Which penicillin?** 'Penicillin' was a family. British material was largely **penicillin F** (2-pentenyl side chain), whereas American corn steep fermentations favoured **penicillin G** (benzyl), because the liquor supplied phenylacetic acid, a side-chain precursor. Adding phenylacetic acid deliberately raised yields: an early case of precursor-directed biosynthesis. Strain improvement followed: Mary Hunt's mouldy-cantaloupe isolate of Penicillium chrysogenum (NRRL 1951) and its X-ray and UV-induced mutants, such as Q-176, raised yields many-fold.

**Structure dispute.** Edward Abraham and Chain proposed the β-lactam structure; Robert Robinson favoured a thiazolidine-oxazolone. Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin's X-ray crystallography (1945) settled it in favour of the β-lactam.

**Mechanism and selectivity.** Penicillins acylate the active-site serine of transpeptidases (**penicillin-binding proteins**) that cross-link peptidoglycan. Tipper and Strominger (1965) proposed that penicillin mimics the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the peptide stem. Humans lack peptidoglycan, so toxicity is low; because killing depends on ongoing wall synthesis, penicillin works best against actively growing bacteria.

**Pharmacokinetics.** Penicillin G is cleared rapidly and largely unchanged, mainly by renal tubular secretion through organic anion transporters, giving a short half-life. Hence the Oxford team recovered penicillin from patients' urine, and **probenecid** was later developed to block tubular secretion and prolong plasma levels.
levels.expert:
Read as a translational project, the Oxford work anticipates problems that still dominate drug development.

**Effect size versus statistics.** The 1940 mouse test used eight animals, yet the effect was so large that no statistics were needed. Early clinical use was a series of uncontrolled cases, defensible only because untreated streptococcal and staphylococcal septicaemia was so predictably lethal. Most modern drugs offer far smaller effects, which is why randomized trials became essential.

**Supply as a clinical variable.** Alexander's relapse showed that limited supply can turn a cure into a failure. The team prioritized children for the 1941 series partly because they needed less material.

**Neurosurgery's stake.** Hugh Cairns, the Australian Nuffield Professor of Surgery at Oxford, used penicillin for infected head wounds and brain abscesses during the war, and Florey travelled with him to North Africa in 1943 to study battlefield wounds. A lesson came quickly: penicillin crosses the intact blood-brain barrier poorly, prompting local and intrathecal use, yet direct application to cortex is epileptogenic because penicillin antagonises **GABA-A receptors**. Topical penicillin later became a standard laboratory method for creating seizure foci.

**Credit.** In August 1942 Fleming treated Harry Lambert, who had streptococcal meningitis, with Oxford-made penicillin, including intrathecal injection. Press coverage, amplified by Almroth Wright's letter to The Times, centred Fleming, while Florey avoided journalists. The Nobel limit of three laureates excluded Heatley; in 1990 Oxford gave him an honorary Doctorate of Medicine, the first awarded to a non-medic in its history.

**Patents.** Chain urged patenting; Florey and the Medical Research Council judged it improper for a medical discovery. Moyer patented fermentation methods, and British firms later paid licence fees, a grievance that helped motivate the creation of the National Research Development Corporation in 1949.

**Open questions.** Penicillin succeeded because wartime governments coordinated academia, agriculture laboratories and industry, paying for scale-up that markets would not. Today discovery is less limiting than economics: new antibiotics are held in reserve, so sales stay low. Pull incentives such as England's subscription model, which pays for access rather than volume, are modern attempts to recreate that coordination.

lessons.title: Waksman, Schatz and Streptomycin Against Tuberculosis

levels.kid:
Tuberculosis, or **TB**, is a sickness that hurts the lungs. Long ago it killed millions of people. The new medicines of the 1930s did not work on it, because the TB germ wears a thick, waxy coat like a raincoat.

In 1943 a young student scientist named **Albert Schatz** worked in his teacher Selman Waksman's lab. He searched through dirt, because tiny soil germs make chemicals to fight each other. He found one that made a germ-fighting chemical called **streptomycin**. It could beat TB!

But there was a problem. If doctors used only streptomycin, some TB germs learned to survive it. Those germs are called resistant. So doctors began giving two or three medicines together. That way the germs struggle to resist, the same idea doctors still use today.
levels.hs:
**Tuberculosis (TB)** is caused by the bacterium *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, identified by Robert Koch in 1882. By the 1940s, sulfa drugs and penicillin were saving lives, but they did little against TB. The TB bacterium has a **thick, waxy cell wall** and grows very slowly, so it shrugged them off.

At Rutgers University, soil microbiologist **Selman Waksman** ran a lab that screened soil microbes called **actinomycetes**. He popularized the word **antibiotic** for a substance made by one microbe that kills or blocks other microbes. His first finds, like actinomycin, were too toxic for patients.

In 1943 his graduate student **Albert Schatz** isolated a strain of ***Streptomyces griseus*** that made **streptomycin**. It killed the TB bacterium and many bacteria that penicillin missed. At the **Mayo Clinic**, William Feldman and Corwin Hinshaw cured TB in guinea pigs, then treated the first human patient in November 1944.

A real example of the drug's impact: in 1948 Britain's **Medical Research Council (MRC)** published a carefully designed trial. Six months after starting, 7% of patients given streptomycin had died, compared with 27% of patients given bed rest alone.

But a warning appeared fast. When streptomycin was used alone, many patients' bacteria became **resistant**. Adding a second drug, **para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS)**, greatly reduced resistance. This launched the rule of **combination therapy** for TB.
levels.college:
Streptomycin was the first effective drug against tuberculosis and a product of a deliberate search strategy, not a lucky accident like penicillin.

**The Waksman screening program.** Waksman's Rutgers group systematically grew soil actinomycetes and tested their products against target bacteria. Earlier hits failed: **actinomycin** (1940) and **streptothricin** (1942) were too toxic. In 1943 Albert Schatz, working in an isolated basement lab with virulent TB cultures, recovered two *Streptomyces griseus* strains, one from heavily manured field soil and one from a chicken's throat swab. The January 1944 paper by Schatz, Bugie and Waksman reported activity against Gram-negative bacteria and *M. tuberculosis*. Merck scaled up production.

**Mechanism.** Streptomycin is an **aminoglycoside**:
- It binds the bacterial **30S ribosomal subunit**, contacting 16S rRNA and ribosomal protein S12.
- It distorts the decoding site, causing codon **misreading** and faulty proteins.
- It is **bactericidal** and poorly absorbed from the gut, so it was injected.
- Main toxicities: damage to **hearing and balance** (the eighth cranial nerve) and the kidneys.

**The 1948 MRC trial.** Statistician **Austin Bradford Hill** designed a trial in pulmonary TB: 55 patients received streptomycin plus bed rest and 52 received bed rest alone. Allocation used random numbers in **sealed envelopes**, and X-rays were read by assessors who did not know the assignment. Deaths at six months were 4 of 55 versus 14 of 52. An untreated control group was considered ethical because too little drug existed for everyone.

**Resistance.** The same trial showed many survivors' bacilli became resistant within months. Jörgen Lehmann's **PAS** combined with streptomycin cut resistance sharply in a 1950 MRC trial, and isoniazid followed in 1952. TB treatment has used **multidrug combinations** ever since.

**The credit dispute.** In 1950 Schatz sued Waksman over patent royalties and recognition. A settlement named him co-discoverer, but the 1952 Nobel Prize went to Waksman alone.
levels.phd:
**Ribosomal mechanism.** Crystal structures of the *Thermus thermophilus* 30S subunit bound to streptomycin (Carter et al., *Nature* 2000, Ramakrishnan lab) showed the drug bridging the 16S rRNA backbone near helices h1, h18, h27 and h44 and contacting **lysine 43 of protein S12**. It stabilizes the ribosome's ambiguous (ram) state, lowering the accuracy of tRNA selection. Mistranslated membrane proteins disrupt the envelope and boost further drug uptake, contributing to bactericidal killing. Gorini's genetic work in the 1960s, including streptomycin-resistant and even streptomycin-**dependent** *E. coli* mutants, helped establish the ribosome as an active proofreading machine.

**Uptake.** Entry of the polycationic drug across the cytoplasmic membrane needs an energy-dependent phase driven by the respiratory **proton-motive force**. Because uptake needs oxygen-driven transport, aminoglycosides are inactive against strict anaerobes.

**Resistance genetics in *M. tuberculosis*.** Mycobacteria carry a single rRNA operon, so one chromosomal point mutation can confer resistance:
- ***rpsL*** (S12), classically K43R and K88R: high-level resistance.
- ***rrs*** (16S rRNA), notably the 530 loop and 912 region.
- ***gidB***, encoding a methyltransferase for 16S G527; loss gives low-level resistance.
There are no transferable plasmids involved; resistance arises by chromosomal mutation plus selection.

**Why combinations work.** Spontaneous streptomycin-resistant mutants occur at roughly 1 in 10^6 bacilli, while a lung cavity may hold 10^8 to 10^9. Monotherapy therefore almost guarantees pre-existing resistant mutants and selects them. If resistance to a second drug arises independently at a similar rate, double-resistant cells occur near 1 in 10^12, beyond the bacillary load. The 1948 and 1950 MRC trials gave the clinical proof.

**Trial methodology.** Hill's design was influential because of **allocation concealment** (preventing selection bias) and **blinded outcome assessment** of radiographs (preventing measurement bias), not only randomization itself.

**Discovery controversy.** Schatz had assigned his rights to the Rutgers Research Foundation, while Waksman held an undisclosed royalty arrangement. The 1950 settlement gave Schatz a small royalty share and co-discoverer status. Historians still debate how much credit a trainee deserves when the strategy is the supervisor's.
levels.expert:
**Neurological legacy.** Before streptomycin, **tuberculous meningitis** was almost uniformly fatal. The MRC's 1948 Lancet report showed survival for the first time, often with intrathecal as well as intramuscular drug, but survivors frequently had deafness, hydrocephalus or cranial nerve palsies. That pattern prefigured today's TB meningitis care, where neurosurgeons still manage hydrocephalus with ventricular drainage or shunting. Streptomycin's poor penetration across uninflamed meninges is one reason it is no longer favored for CNS TB.

**Pharmacogenomic pitfall.** The mitochondrial **12S rRNA m.1555A>G** variant makes the human mitochondrial ribosome more bacterial-like at the aminoglycoside binding site, and carriers can develop profound hearing loss after aminoglycoside exposure. Some neonatal units now use rapid point-of-care genotyping before giving aminoglycosides. The mechanism explains selective toxicity: high-fidelity eukaryotic cytosolic ribosomes differ from bacterial ones, but mitochondria preserve their bacterial ancestry.

**Where streptomycin stands now.** It remains a drug of choice, alone or with a tetracycline, for **plague** and **tularemia**, and it is used in some brucellosis regimens, though gentamicin often substitutes. For TB its role has shrunk. Widespread resistance and irreversible ototoxicity led WHO (2018 to 2022) to shift **drug-resistant TB** toward all-oral regimens such as BPaLM (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin), retiring most injectables.

**Diagnostics.** Molecular tests like Xpert MTB/RIF detect rifampicin resistance directly. Streptomycin resistance is less reliably predicted because *gidB* polymorphisms include lineage markers not linked to resistance, a recurring problem when genotype is used to infer phenotype.

**Research ethics and credit.** The Schatz case is now taught as a cautionary tale about trainee recognition and undisclosed financial interests. Rutgers honored Schatz with its medal in 1994.

**Open questions.** The Waksman soil-screening approach later gave neomycin and helped define antibiotics' golden age, then slowed as rediscovery of known compounds dominated. Genome mining of silent biosynthetic gene clusters and culturing previously unculturable soil bacteria (as in the 2015 discovery of teixobactin) are attempts to restart the pipeline Waksman's lab began.

lessons.title: Early Warnings: Penicillinase to the First MRSA (1961)

levels.kid:
Penicillin was a superhero medicine. It could beat germs that used to make people very sick. But germs are sneaky.

Even before penicillin was given to patients, two scientists found something surprising. Some germs make a special tool, like tiny scissors, that can cut penicillin and break it. This tool is called **penicillinase**.

When doctors used lots of penicillin, the germs without scissors died. The germs with scissors lived and made more germs just like them. Soon, many hospital germs could beat penicillin.

Scientists made a new medicine called **methicillin**, which the scissors could not cut. But in 1961, a scientist named Patricia Jevons found germs that could beat it too. We call them **MRSA**. It taught doctors to use germ medicine carefully.
levels.hs:
Bacteria fought back against penicillin almost as soon as it arrived. A germ's ability to survive a drug that should kill it is called **antibiotic resistance**.

Penicillin's key feature is a strained, four-membered ring of atoms called the **beta-lactam ring**. In 1940, before penicillin had been given to patients, Edward Abraham and Ernst Chain discovered that some bacteria make an enzyme that cuts this ring open and destroys the drug. They named it **penicillinase**. Today it is classed among the **beta-lactamases**.

Resistance spreads by **natural selection**. Penicillin kills the sensitive bacteria, but a few cells that already carry penicillinase survive and multiply. The drug doesn't create resistance; it picks the winners.

A real example: at Hammersmith Hospital in London, **Mary Barber** tracked **Staphylococcus aureus** ('staph'), a common cause of wound and skin infections. Penicillin-resistant staph rose from about 14% of hospital isolates in 1946 to about 59% by 1948. She showed that resistant strains were spreading from patient to patient, rather than sensitive germs being transformed by the drug.

Chemists responded with **methicillin** (introduced 1959-60), a new penicillin built to resist breakdown by penicillinase. Within about a year, in 1961, **Patricia Jevons** reported staph that survived methicillin too: the first **MRSA**, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
levels.college:
**How penicillin works.** Penicillin and its relatives (the beta-lactams) mimic the D-Ala-D-Ala end of cell wall building blocks and bind **penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)**, the transpeptidase enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan. Without cross-links the wall weakens and the growing bacterium bursts.

**Mechanism 1: destroy the drug.** Penicillinase, a beta-lactamase, hydrolyzes the amide bond of the beta-lactam ring, producing inactive penicilloic acid. Milestones:
- 1940: Abraham and Chain describe penicillinase in Escherichia coli, before clinical use.
- 1944: William Kirby extracts penicillin-inactivating material from resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
- 1945: In his Nobel lecture, Fleming warns that giving too little drug could breed resistant microbes.
- 1946-48: Mary Barber documents resistant staph rising to a majority of Hammersmith isolates and spreading by cross-infection.
- 1950s: an epidemic staph strain, phage type 80/81, causes hospital and community outbreaks across several continents.

In staph, penicillinase is encoded by the gene **blaZ**, usually on plasmids, so it can move between strains.

**The chemists' answer.** In 1957 Beecham scientists isolated **6-aminopenicillanic acid (6-APA)**, the bare penicillin core (published 1959). Chemists could now attach new side chains. Methicillin (brand name Celbenin) carries a bulky dimethoxyphenyl group that physically shields the beta-lactam ring from penicillinase.

**Mechanism 2: change the target.** In 1961 Patricia Jevons at the Public Health Laboratory Service in London reported 3 Celbenin-resistant isolates among 5,440 staph strains screened. Decades later the mechanism was clarified: MRSA carries **mecA**, which encodes **PBP2a**, an extra wall-building transpeptidase with low affinity for most beta-lactams. It keeps cross-linking the wall while the normal PBPs are blocked, so no enzyme needs to destroy the drug at all. Methicillin itself is no longer used clinically, but the name MRSA stuck.
levels.phd:
**Selection, not instruction.** In the 1940s many assumed drugs 'trained' bacteria to resist. Luria and Delbrück's fluctuation test (1943) showed that bacterial resistance to phage arises by random mutation before exposure, and Joshua and Esther Lederberg's replica plating (1952) showed antibiotic-resistant colonies present in populations never exposed to the drug. Abraham and Chain's 1940 penicillinase, found before clinical use, fits this picture: the drug selects pre-existing variants.

**Penicillinase biochemistry.** Staphylococcal PC1 penicillinase is an Ambler class A serine beta-lactamase. Its active-site serine attacks the beta-lactam carbonyl, forming an acyl-enzyme that is rapidly hydrolyzed, unlike the long-lived acyl-enzyme formed with PBPs. That difference in deacylation rate is the crux: PBPs and serine beta-lactamases are evolutionarily related, and the beta-lactamase has become fast at releasing the drug. blaZ is inducible: the membrane sensor BlaR1 detects beta-lactams and triggers inactivation of the repressor BlaI. Richard Novick's work in the 1960s established that blaZ is typically plasmid-borne, often within transposon Tn552.

**Horizontal transfer.** In Japan around 1959-60, Ochiai, Akiba and colleagues showed that multidrug resistance in Shigella could be transferred to E. coli by conjugation; Tsutomu Watanabe's 1963 review brought these 'R factors' to Western attention. Resistance was a gene-sharing problem, not just a mutation problem.

**MRSA's distinct mechanism.** Hartman and Tomasz (1984) identified PBP2a, and mecA was cloned soon after. mecA sits on a mobile genomic island, the **staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec (SCCmec)**, which integrates at the orfX locus via cassette chromosome recombinases (ccrAB or ccrC). mecA is regulated by MecR1/MecI, homologues of BlaR1/BlaI, which can also control it. Its ancestor appears to derive from the Staphylococcus sciuri group (now Mammaliicoccus) and S. fleurettii, animal-associated species.

**Detection nuance.** Early MRSA was often **heteroresistant**: only a minority of cells expressed high-level resistance, so routine tests could miss it. Incubating at 30 °C or adding salt improved detection, an early lesson that a resistance phenotype depends on test conditions.
levels.expert:
**Genomics rewrote the 1961 story.** Harkins and colleagues (2017) sequenced Jevons' original isolates, including NCTC 10442, alongside archival strains. Dating the phylogeny suggested mecA, on SCCmec type I, was acquired around the mid-1940s, roughly 14 years before methicillin. The likely selective driver was penicillin itself, not methicillin; methicillin merely revealed a resistance already circulating. This early 'archaic' clone (ST250 and its descendant ST247, clonal complex 8) spread through European hospitals, notably in Denmark, during the 1960s, then declined in the 1970s for reasons still debated.

**Resistance before medicine.** Larsen et al. (2022, Nature) showed that mecC-MRSA in European hedgehogs emerged about two centuries ago, selected by the dermatophyte Trichophyton erinacei, which secretes beta-lactams on hedgehog skin. mecC is a divergent mecA homologue, so mecA-specific PCR can miss it; cefoxitin-based phenotypic testing or assays that cover mecC are needed.

**The first stewardship experiment.** In the late 1950s Barber's Hammersmith team restricted routine penicillin and tetracycline use and favoured combination therapy for serious staph infections; in 1960 they reported a fall in penicillin-resistant staph. When selection pressure eases, resistant strains can lose ground, consistent with fitness costs and clonal replacement, though reversal is usually slow and partial.

**Laboratory legacy.**
- Methicillin is no longer marketed; oxacillin and cefoxitin replaced it in testing, cefoxitin being a stronger inducer of mecA expression.
- PBP2a latex agglutination and molecular assays are rapid but must match the circulating mec genes.
- Heteroresistance still complicates borderline results.

**Therapeutic legacy.** Because PBP2a resists most beta-lactams, MRSA treatment shifted to non-beta-lactams such as vancomycin. Anti-MRSA cephalosporins (ceftaroline, ceftobiprole) were later designed to bind PBP2a; ceftaroline also binds an allosteric site that opens PBP2a's active site.

**Open questions.** Why do some MRSA clones go pandemic while others fade? How much do animal reservoirs and non-antibiotic selectors, such as metals and biocides, contribute? The 1940-1961 arc is a lasting warning: resistance often predates a drug and surfaces quickly once use scales up.

keyPoints: Abraham and Chain described penicillinase in 1940, before penicillin reached patients
Penicillinase (a beta-lactamase) cuts the beta-lactam ring, inactivating penicillin
Drugs select pre-existing resistant bacteria; they do not instruct them
Mary Barber showed resistant staph spreading between hospital patients (1946-48)
Methicillin resisted penicillinase, but Jevons reported MRSA in 1961
MRSA uses mecA-encoded PBP2a, a target bypass rather than drug destruction

test.q: What does the enzyme penicillinase do to penicillin?
choices: Blocks it from crossing the wall
Pumps it back out of the cell
test.explain: Penicillinase hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring, destroying the drug. It is an enzyme that breaks the drug, not a pump or a barrier.

test.q: Abraham and Chain's 1940 report of penicillinase was striking mainly because it came:
choices: After decades of routine penicillin use
From a hospital outbreak of staph infection
Before penicillin was given to patients
From studying mold that grew in soil samples
test.explain: The enzyme was found before penicillin's clinical use, showing that resistance mechanisms already existed in nature.

test.q: What did Mary Barber show about penicillin-resistant staph at Hammersmith Hospital?
choices: Resistant strains spread from patient to patient
Resistance began in tuberculosis wards first
Penicillin turned sensitive cells into resistant ones
Patients' own cells were making penicillinase
test.explain: Barber showed that resistant strains were spreading by cross-infection, not that the drug converted sensitive bacteria.

test.q: Why did penicillin-resistant staph become common in hospitals so quickly?
choices: Penicillin taught bacteria to build new enzymes
Patients developed allergies that blocked the drug
Penicillin lost potency when stored in hospitals
Sensitive cells died and resistant ones multiplied
test.explain: This is natural selection: the drug kills sensitive bacteria and leaves resistant ones to take over. It does not teach bacteria anything.

test.q: Methicillin was introduced around 1959-60 mainly to:
choices: Act as a vaccine against staph
test.explain: Methicillin's bulky side chain shields its beta-lactam ring from penicillinase, so it worked against penicillinase-producing staph.

test.q: Who reported the first methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in 1961?
test.explain: Patricia Jevons of the Public Health Laboratory Service reported Celbenin-resistant staph in 1961. Barber had tracked penicillin resistance earlier.

test.q: How does MRSA resist methicillin?
choices: It pumps methicillin out of the cell
It uses an altered wall enzyme, PBP2a
It hides inside human white blood cells
test.explain: MRSA makes PBP2a, which binds beta-lactams poorly and keeps building the wall. Extra penicillinase would not work, because methicillin resists it.

test.q: What is penicillin's normal target in bacteria?
test.explain: Penicillin binds penicillin-binding proteins, the transpeptidases that cross-link peptidoglycan in the cell wall.

test.q: Why did Beecham's isolation of 6-APA (the penicillin core) matter?
choices: It was the first antibiotic made by a mold
It made penicillin safe for allergic patients
Chemists could attach new side chains to it
It killed tuberculosis better than streptomycin
test.explain: 6-APA allowed semisynthetic penicillins such as methicillin, built by adding new side chains to the core.

test.q: Which bacterium, often called 'staph', did Mary Barber track in hospital patients?
test.explain: Barber followed penicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus, a common cause of wound and skin infections.

test.q: Penicillinase belongs to the family of beta-___ enzymes.
test.explain: Beta-lactamases break the beta-lactam ring found in penicillins and related drugs.

test.q: MRSA's resistance gene, ___, codes for the protein PBP2a.
test.explain: mecA, carried on the mobile element SCCmec, encodes PBP2a, which has low affinity for most beta-lactams.

kidTest.q: In the story, penicillinase is like what?
choices: A key that lets medicine inside
A shield that protects the person
kidTest.explain: Penicillinase works like scissors that cut penicillin and break it.

kidTest.q: What happened when doctors used lots of penicillin?
choices: The germs slowly turned into good germs
Germs with the scissors lived and grew
kidTest.explain: Germs without scissors died, but germs with scissors lived and made more germs like them.

kidTest.q: What new medicine did scientists make that the scissors could not cut?
kidTest.explain: Methicillin was built so penicillinase could not cut it.

kidTest.q: What did MRSA teach doctors?
choices: To keep one medicine for years
To give germ medicine for colds
kidTest.explain: Germs can learn to beat medicines, so doctors must use them carefully.

kidTest.q: Germs that can beat methicillin are called M _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: MRSA was first found by Patricia Jevons in 1961.

advancedTest.q: Penicillinase was described in 1940, and genomics dates MRSA's mecA acquisition to the mid-1940s, before methicillin existed. What best follows?
choices: Resistance needs decades of drug exposure to appear
Penicillin directly causes new resistance mutations
Methicillin use in hospitals created the mecA gene
Resistance genes can predate the drug they defeat
advancedTest.explain: Both findings show resistance determinants existing before the relevant drug was in use. Drugs select such variants; they do not create them.

advancedTest.q: Methicillin's bulky side chain blocks penicillinase. Why does this design fail against MRSA?
choices: MRSA pumps out drugs that carry bulky side chains
PBP2a binds the drug poorly and keeps building wall
MRSA makes a bigger penicillinase that fits the chain
MRSA lacks a cell wall and so lacks the target
advancedTest.explain: MRSA bypasses the drug's target rather than destroying the drug. Shielding the ring from hydrolysis is irrelevant when PBP2a ignores the drug.

advancedTest.q: A lab screens S. aureus with a mecA-only PCR. Which isolate could be wrongly called methicillin-susceptible?
choices: One that is heteroresistant to oxacillin
One producing high levels of penicillinase
One carrying the divergent homolog mecC
One with SCCmec type I from the 1960s
advancedTest.explain: mecC is divergent enough that mecA-specific PCR can miss it. Heteroresistant and SCCmec type I strains still carry mecA, and penicillinase alone does not confer methicillin resistance.

advancedTest.q: After Barber's 1960 Hammersmith policy restricted certain antibiotics, penicillin resistance among staph fell. The best interpretation is:
choices: Hospital staph stopped exchanging plasmids with each other
Restriction caused bacteria to destroy their resistance genes
Remaining drugs reversed penicillinase into an inactive form
Resistant strains lose ground when selection pressure eases
advancedTest.explain: Removing selective pressure lets less burdened or competing strains replace resistant ones, consistent with fitness costs and clonal replacement. Bacteria do not deliberately discard genes.
